title: The Radium Girls
summary: Josh and Chuck open with Chuck's COVID-19 diagnosis and a vaccination plea, then examine the Radium Girls: young women who painted glow-in-the-dark watch dials with radium paint in the 1910s and 1920s. They cover the era's belief that radium was a cure-all (including Radithor water), the lip-pointing technique that led to ingestion, and how radium lodged in the bones. The episode describes the United States Radium Corporation's cover-up, including its alteration of the Drinker report, the death of Molly Maggia, and the investigation by Dr. Harrison Martland. It then covers the five plaintiffs' lawsuit and settlement, the Radium Dial lawsuit in Ottawa, Illinois, and the regulatory changes that followed. The episode closes with a listener mail about the Grand Ole Opry.
topics: glow in the dark watch dials

segments.title: COVID update and episode setup
segments.summary: Chuck announces he has COVID-19 and urges listeners to get vaccinated. The hosts introduce the Radium Girls, mention the Kate Moore book and a 2018 film, and note that Jerry is not present.

segments.title: Radium's history and the glow-in-the-dark craze
segments.summary: Radium is introduced as a 1910s-1920s cure-all, with products such as Radithor water. The Curies' discovery and early research are discussed, along with the split between academic caution and industry-funded promotion. Glow-in-the-dark watch dials became a fad, and companies hired very young women, including girls as young as fourteen, to paint them.
topics: glow in the dark watch dials

segments.title: Radium Girls' pay and working conditions
segments.summary: Dial painters were well paid for the era and worked with a very expensive material. The hosts describe the women's glowing hair and clothes, and the 'ghost girls' nickname.

segments.title: Undark paint and lip pointing
segments.summary: The painters mixed their own Undark paint from radium dust and used lip pointing to get fine brush tips, which meant ingesting radium. Frederick Hoffman's calculation of daily intake is mentioned. Radium behaves like calcium in the body and settles in the bones.

segments.title: Company denials and corporate culture
segments.summary: The company's private research claimed radium was harmless, and a 1916 publication from the Radium Publishing Company made fairy-tale claims. Workers were handled carelessly, while the head chemist handled radium without protection.

segments.title: Molly Maggia's death and the syphilis blame
segments.summary: Molly Maggia's jaw was removed by a dentist after radium-related abscesses. She later died after an abscess reached her jugular vein. The company blamed syphilis, and the hosts contrast this with phossy jaw in matchmakers.

segments.title: Cover-up and the Drinker report
segments.summary: Twelve women had died and about fifty were ill, but production continued. An independent investigation by Cecil and Katherine Drinker linked the illnesses to radium. The company blamed hysteria, altered the report, and used a fake doctor to examine a painter.

segments.title: Harrison Martland's investigation and the five plaintiffs
segments.summary: After a chemist died, Dr. Harrison Martland investigated with Sabin von Sochocky, who found radioactivity in the workers. Five women, including Grace Fryar, sued with lawyer Raymond Berry. The press supported them, and they settled for ten thousand dollars each plus an annual payment.

segments.title: Radium Dial lawsuit, regulation, and Ottawa cleanup
segments.summary: The Radium Dial company knew about the workers' exposure and suppressed it. Women plaintiffs led a suit there. The hosts describe later workplace-safety and food and drug laws, and radioactive rubble spread across Ottawa, Illinois.

segments.title: Listener mail: Grand Ole Opry
segments.summary: A listener from Nashville responds to the Grand Ole Opry episode, recalling local memories and the city's bachelor party scene.

segments.title: Outro
segments.summary: The hosts give the contact email and sign off.
